idiom_name: use-prefixed hook functions composed from useState/useEffect/useContext
implementation_notes: In React the pattern is the native idiom rather than a structure to build: a plain function whose name starts with use may call the built-in hooks (useState, useEffect, useContext) and is invoked at the top level of a component, and the returned tuple or object replaces the mixin, higher-order-component and render-prop wrappers that pre-16.8 code used for the same reuse. State slots and effect cleanup are owned by React, so the same unit is shared by unrelated components without wrapping their tree, and units compose because a custom Hook may call other Hooks. Keep the classic wrapper forms only when the reuse is genuinely structural - a layout or prop-injection shell - rather than stateful behaviour.
pitfalls: Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level: inside a condition, loop, event handler or plain function the call-order state mapping shifts and state slots are displaced.
Effects capture the render's values; without correct dependency arrays and stable callbacks a subscription keeps a stale setter or restarts on every render.
Two components calling the same hook get independent state - sharing requires a context or an external store, not another hook call.

variants.name: Vue Composition API composables
variants.implementation_notes: Vue's own documentation defines a composable as a function that leverages the Composition API to encapsulate and reuse stateful logic: ref() holds the state, computed() derives values, watchEffect() re-runs on reactive inputs, and onMounted/onUnmounted register the side-effect lifecycle. Composables nest, so complex behaviour is assembled from small units just as components assemble an application - the functional replacement for options-API mixins - and each component instance calling the composable receives its own copies of the state, with the docs pointing to the state-management chapter when shared state is actually wanted.
pitfalls: Lifecycle registration helpers such as onMounted only work when called synchronously during setup; invoking them from an async callback silently loses the registration.
Every component instance gets its own reactive state copies - expecting a composable to share state between components is the documented misuse and needs the state-management pattern instead.
